eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 1, Lesson 4
subtitle: Three ways to hold more than one value — and when each one is the right tool.

code:
line_totals = [259.98, 249.50, 79.00]

line_totals.append(129.99)     # add a new total to the end
print(line_totals)              # [259.98, 249.50, 79.00, 129.99]

print(line_totals[0])           # 259.98 — first item, index 0
print(line_totals[-1])          # 129.99 — last item
print(len(line_totals))         # 4
caption: Negative indexing ([-1]) is the normal way to grab "the most recent one" without knowing the count.

code:
order_record = (1001, "Dana Whitfield", "Shipped")
print(order_record[0])    # 1001
# order_record[0] = 9999  # TypeError

def min_and_max(values):
    return min(values), max(values)   # returns a tuple

lowest, highest = min_and_max([259.98, 249.50, 79.00])
print(lowest, highest)   # 79.0 259.98
caption: A tuple signals "fixed, complete record" — and it's how a function returns more than one value.
